title: Traffic Banking 101
description: The way Dchessking runs paid traffic at Zedapex: price every lead, buy the right signal and keep working the lead after the join. Six short lessons that set the rules every other course builds on.

lessons.title: Traffic is capital

steps.p: Most new buyers treat ad spend as a bill they pay and forget. Traffic banking treats every dollar as capital you put to work and expect back with a return.

d.s: Leads, data and depositors you keep

steps.h: Two ways to look at spend
steps.p: The same budget gets managed very differently depending on which column you think in.
Spend buys leads. Some leads become depositors. Payouts fund the next round, with a margin on top.
Even a losing test buys something. The question is whether you capture it and use it on the next campaign.
Example: every dollar spent came back as $1.40 in payouts over 30 days. That one number tells you whether to add capital or pull it.
Dchessking on the habit that cost him most in his early years.
steps.d: I burnt money for a long time because I counted spend as a cost. When I started pricing every lead like an asset, every decision changed.

steps.p: Four habits that turn spend into something you can measure and grow.
d: Write down your payout per FTD
Track spend by ad set every day
Review return per dollar every Friday

takeaways: Ad spend is capital you expect back with a return.
Every test buys leads, data or lessons. Capture them.
Return per dollar decides when to add or pull budget.
lessons.action: Start a sheet with five columns: date, spend, joins, FTDs and payouts. Fill it every day for the next 7 days.

quiz.q: In traffic banking, what decides whether you add budget?
options: How much each dollar brings back
How many likes the ad gets
How long the ad has been running
quiz.explain: Capital goes where it returns money. Cheap clicks and likes can look good while returning nothing.

lessons.title: Price every lead

steps.h: Know the price before you buy
steps.p: A bank never lends without knowing the rate. You should never buy a lead without knowing the most it is worth to you.
FTD means first-time deposit. Multiply the payout per FTD by the share of joins that deposit, and you get the most one join is worth.
Example: the network pays $60 per FTD and 4 in every 100 joins deposit. Each join is worth $2.40 to you before any profit.
Example: to keep a 30% margin, bid at 70% of break-even. Your target cost per join becomes $1.68.
Illustration: three ad sets measured against a $2.40 break-even. Ad sets A and B make money. Ad set C loses on every join.
Most buyers know their cost per lead. Far fewer know what that lead is worth.
steps.d: If you cannot say the most you would pay for a lead, every click you buy is a guess made with real money.

steps.p: Do this once per offer and geo, then update it as your own data comes in.
d: Use your own FTD rate once you have it
Set a target cost per join
Write it at the top of the campaign sheet

takeaways: Payout × FTD rate = the most a join is worth.
Bid below break-even so there is room for profit.
Replace guessed FTD rates with your own data fast.
lessons.action: Work out the break-even and target cost per join for your main offer. Write both numbers where you check results every day.

quiz.q: Payout is $50 per FTD and 5% of joins deposit. What is the break-even cost per join?
quiz.explain: $50 × 5% = $2.50. Above $2.50 per join you lose money before counting any other costs.

lessons.title: Signals over clicks

steps.p: The ad platform looks for more people like the ones you report. Report clicks and it finds clickers. Report deposits and it looks for depositors.

d.s: Report the event you want more of

steps.p: Illustration: most clicks never join, and few joins deposit. Optimising for the top of this funnel buys the wrong people.
A click costs less to buy, but it tells the algorithm very little about who pays.
When a real join or deposit happens, your tracking sends it to Meta from a server. Meta matches it to the click and adjusts who it shows ads to.
Deeper events are worth more but happen less often. Lesson 4 of the tracking course shows how to pick one.
Dchessking on why tracking comes before scaling.
steps.d: Every buyer needs clean signals. Without them, the algorithm spends your money finding the wrong people.

steps.p: Small fixes here change who Meta finds for you.
d: Send only real joins and deposits
Pick one optimisation event per ad set

takeaways: The platform finds more of whatever you report.
Clicks are cheap signals. Joins and deposits are valuable ones.
Send clean, real events from a server.
lessons.action: List the event each of your live ad sets optimises for. Move any ad set still optimising for clicks to a deeper event.

quiz.q: Your ad set optimises for link clicks. What is the likely result?
options: Meta finds people likely to deposit
Meta finds people likely to click, whether or not they deposit
quiz.explain: The algorithm hunts for the event you report. Click optimisation finds clickers, and many of them never join or deposit.

lessons.title: Creative velocity

steps.p: Targeting on Meta is broad now, so the ad itself decides who stops. The hook picks your audience before any setting does.
Example: a small team might ship five new creatives a week per offer. The exact number matters less than keeping the pace every week.
Brief on Monday, produce midweek, launch, read the data, then use what you learned in the next brief.

steps.h: Change one thing at a time
steps.p: If you change everything at once, you cannot tell what worked. Test one variable per round.
Illustration: in a typical batch, most creatives fail, a few hold, and one may carry the account. Volume is how you find that one.
Every winning ad slows down eventually.
steps.d: Winners die. The buyer with the next creative ready is the one whose account keeps running.

steps.p: A pipeline means you are never waiting for creatives when a winner fades.
d: Keep a swipe file of hooks
Name every file by angle and hook
Switch off clear losers within 3 days

takeaways: On broad targeting, the creative picks the audience.
A steady weekly pace beats occasional big batches.
Test one variable at a time so results teach you something.
lessons.action: Write five hooks for your best angle and brief them as five new ads to launch next week.

quiz.q: Why does creative volume matter so much on Meta today?
options: Meta charges less for new ads
Most creatives lose, so you need many tests to find winners
Old ads are deleted after a week
Meta requires five ads per ad set
quiz.explain: Most tests fail and winners fade. A steady flow of new creatives is how you keep finding the next one.

lessons.title: Kill rules and scale rules

steps.p: Feelings make bad budget calls. Write the rules before launch, then let the numbers make the decision.
Example: if an ad set spends twice your target CPA with zero FTDs, switch it off. CPA means cost per acquisition, here the cost of one FTD.
Example rules. Adjust the numbers to your offer and your own data.
Every ad set gets one of three verdicts each day. Nothing gets left running out of hope.
Many buyers raise a winning budget by about 20% at a time and wait a day or two before the next raise. Big jumps can push an ad set back into learning.
Dchessking on the early mistakes that rules removed.
steps.d: Most of the money I burnt early went into ads I knew were dead. I kept hoping. Written rules took the hoping out.

steps.p: Put them in the same sheet as your numbers so they are applied the same way every day.
d: Target CPA and max cost per join
Kill rule with a spend limit
Scale rule with a time window
How much to raise and how often

takeaways: Write kill and scale rules before launch.
Give every ad set a verdict every day: kill, hold or scale.
Scale winners in small steps.
lessons.action: Write one kill rule and one scale rule for your current campaign and apply them at the same time every day this week.

quiz.q: Target CPA is $25. Under the example rule, when do you kill an ad set with no FTDs?
quiz.explain: The example rule is 2 × target CPA with zero FTDs. 2 × $25 = $50.

lessons.title: The money is in the follow-up

steps.p: Paying for a join and then going quiet wastes the spend. What happens in the next two weeks decides whether that join pays you back.
Illustration: people drop at every step after they join. Each step you improve lifts everything below it.
Illustration: total deposits from one week of joins, with and without a follow-up plan. The gap opens after day one.
Each message has one job. Welcome, build trust, teach, make the offer, then remind.
Use every place you can reach the person, each for its own job.
Dchessking on where buyers lose the most money.
steps.d: Paying for a join and then ignoring the person is the most expensive habit in this business.

steps.p: The Telegram course covers each of these in detail.
d: Welcome message in under a minute
Reply to every DM within 5 minutes

takeaways: Deposits keep coming for days after the join if you follow up.
Improve each step after the join and everything below improves.
Track deposits by the date people joined.
lessons.action: Write your welcome message and the next three follow-up messages. Schedule them for every new join this week.

quiz.q: Two buyers pay the same cost per join. Buyer B follows up for 14 days and Buyer A does not. What should Buyer B expect?
options: The same deposits as Buyer A
More deposits from the same joins
quiz.explain: Same joins, same cost. Follow-up raises how many of those joins deposit, which lowers the real cost per FTD.

title: Tracking that tells the truth
description: Pixels, the Conversions API, postbacks and Telegram attribution in plain English. Learn to send the right signal and read your numbers without fooling yourself.

lessons.title: Pixel vs Conversions API

steps.p: The pixel runs in the browser. Ad blockers, in-app browsers, privacy settings and slow phones all stop some events reaching Meta.
The Conversions API, or CAPI, sends events from your server straight to Meta. Most setups use both.
Someone acts, your server records it, sends it to Meta, and Meta matches it to the person who saw your ad.
The more of these you send with each event, the more events Meta can tie back to an ad. Only send personal data you have consent to use.
d: IP and user agent|from the request

steps.p: If browser and server both send the same purchase, Meta needs to know it is one event. A shared event_id tells it so.
A Telegram join happens inside the Telegram app, where no pixel can run. Server-side events are the only way to report it, which lesson 3 covers.

takeaways: The pixel misses events. CAPI sends them from your server.
Run both with a shared event_id so nothing counts twice.
Telegram joins can only be reported server-side.
lessons.action: Open Events Manager and check whether your main event arrives from browser, server or both, and whether deduplication is working.

quiz.q: Why give the pixel event and the CAPI event the same event_id?
options: To make the event count double
So Meta counts them as one event
To hide the event from Meta
It is required for the pixel to load
quiz.explain: The shared event_id lets Meta deduplicate. Without it, one action can be counted twice and your results look better than they are.

lessons.title: Postbacks and sub IDs

steps.p: The affiliate network sees registrations and deposits. You see clicks. A postback is the network calling your tracker to say which click turned into money.

d.b: Postback = the network calls you back

steps.p: Your click ID rides along in the offer link, comes back in the postback, and ties the deposit to the exact ad.
Sub IDs are blank slots in the offer link for your own data. Names vary by network: sub1, subid, aff_sub, clickid.
At minimum: your click ID, the event type and often the payout. Your tracker joins it to the spend on that click.
Without sub IDs you know your totals. With them you know which ad earned them.

b.title: With sub IDs
items: Cost per FTD per ad set

steps.p: Test end to end before you spend real money.
d: Pass your click ID in sub1
Test with a real sign-up first

takeaways: A postback tells you which click produced a deposit.
Sub IDs carry your click, campaign and ad into the offer link.
Test the full loop before scaling spend.
lessons.action: Ask your network manager for postback documentation and send one test registration through your link with a sub1 value you can find later.

quiz.q: What is the main job of sub1 in most setups?
options: Carry your click ID so the postback can be matched
quiz.explain: sub1 usually carries your click ID. When the postback returns it, your tracker knows exactly which click deposited.

lessons.title: Telegram attribution

steps.p: When someone taps your ad and opens Telegram, the browser trail ends. Without extra work you cannot tell which ad brought which member.

d.s: The join happens where no pixel runs

steps.p: The fix: create a fresh invite link for each visitor and store their click ID beside it. When that link is used, you know which click joined.
A single link in every ad gives you a member count. Unique links give you a member count per ad.

b.title: One link per click
items: Each join tied to a click

steps.p: With admin approval on the link, each person sends a request. Your bot sees who asked, through which link, and decides.
Illustration: tracking each step shows where you lose people between the ad and a confirmed join.
Joinvoo does this job: a unique link per click, join requests handled, and each real join sent to Meta, TikTok and Snapchat server-side. You can also build it yourself with a bot and a database.

d.b: One link per click, one event per join

steps.p: Whichever way you build it, these five pieces need to be in place.
d: Click ID stored with the link
Real joins sent as server events

takeaways: A shared invite link hides which ad brought each member.
A unique link per click ties every join to its ad.
Join requests let you check people before counting them.
lessons.action: Count how many of your live ads use the same invite link. Plan how to give each click its own link, with your own bot or with Joinvoo.

quiz.q: Why create a unique invite link for each click?
options: So each join can be matched to the ad click that caused it
quiz.explain: A link tied to one click ID means every join that uses it can be credited to the right ad, campaign and creative.

lessons.title: Choosing the optimisation event

steps.p: The optimisation event is the action Meta tries to get more of. Too deep and it never learns. Too shallow and it buys junk.
Meta's learning phase needs roughly 50 optimisation events per ad set within 7 days. Below that, delivery tends to stay unstable.

d.label: optimisation events per ad set in 7 days

steps.p: Example: a $100 daily budget is $700 a week. At $25 per FTD that buys 28 FTDs, short of 50, so FTD is too deep for this ad set.
Illustration with the same $700 week: joins at $1.50, registrations at $6 and FTDs at $25. Only joins and registrations reach 50.
Climb the ladder as your volume grows. Each step down is closer to money and harder to hit.
Start where you can hit about 50 a week, then try the next event once volume allows.
Do the volume maths before you pick an event. Fixing it after the ad set stalls costs money.
d: Pick the deepest event you can hit 50 of
Leave it alone once learning ends
Combine ad sets if volume is thin

takeaways: Meta needs roughly 50 optimisation events per ad set in 7 days.
Divide weekly budget by cost per event to check volume.
Pick the deepest event you can reach that volume on.
lessons.action: For each live ad set, divide weekly budget by cost per optimisation event. Note any ad set below 50 and plan a fix.

quiz.q: Weekly budget is $1,000 and cost per registration is $10. Can this ad set optimise for registrations?
options: Yes, it gets about 100 registrations a week
quiz.explain: $1,000 ÷ $10 = 100 registrations a week, well above the rough guide of 50.

lessons.title: Reading your numbers

steps.p: Impressions and likes feel good but pay nothing. Cost per FTD and ROAS tell you whether the money is working.

d.s: Cost per FTD and ROAS decide

steps.p: Example: $600 of spend produced 20 first deposits, so each FTD cost $30.
ROAS is return on ad spend: revenue divided by spend. Example: $900 of payouts from $600 of spend is 1.5, so $1.50 back per $1.
Illustration: a cohort is everyone who joined in the same week. On RevShare its revenue keeps growing after day zero. Compare cohorts at the same age.
Group results by join week, then check value at fixed ages so weeks are comparable.
Keep the left column for diagnosis. Make decisions on the right column.
Read the same numbers at the same time so changes stand out.

takeaways: Cost per FTD = spend ÷ FTDs.
ROAS = revenue ÷ spend.
Judge cohorts at the same age to compare fairly.
lessons.action: Build a cohort table: one row per join week, columns for spend, FTDs, day 7 revenue and day 30 revenue.

quiz.q: You spent $400 and earned $500 in payouts. What is your ROAS?
quiz.explain: ROAS = revenue ÷ spend = $500 ÷ $400 = 1.25, so $1.25 back for every $1.

lessons.title: Fake leads and how to filter them

steps.p: Bots, click farms, paid-to-join users and stray taps all show up as leads. If you report them as conversions, Meta learns to buy more of them.
None of these prove fraud alone. Together they are worth a closer look.
Illustration: raw joins after each filter. The bottom number is the one worth reporting to Meta.
Check each join first, then send only the ones that pass. A short delay is fine.
Start with the first two. Add the rest as your volume grows.
d: Compare network FTDs with your joins

steps.p: Clean reporting can make your cost per join look higher. It is closer to the truth, and that is what the algorithm needs.

takeaways: Fake joins reported as conversions teach Meta to find more fakes.
Filter duplicates and instant leavers before reporting.
Check your joins against network FTDs regularly.
lessons.action: Pull last week's joins and count duplicates and people who left within 24 hours. Decide which filter to add first.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid sending every raw join to Meta as a conversion?
options: Meta learns from junk joins and finds more of them
Meta rejects more than 100 events a day
quiz.explain: The algorithm copies what you report. Junk in the signal means junk in the next round of traffic.

title: Creatives that print
description: Hooks, formats, local language and a weekly testing rhythm for paid social. Learn to make ads people stop for and to spot when a winner is wearing out.

lessons.title: Hooks in the first seconds

steps.p: People scroll fast. If the opening does not stop them, nothing after it gets seen.

d.s: The rest is for people who stayed

steps.p: Six openings that work across verticals. Each one gives the viewer a reason to stay.
Most weak hooks spend the first seconds on branding or warm-up.
Name who it is for, say the problem, promise something honest, show proof, ask for one action.
Illustration: share of viewers still watching. Most of the loss happens before second three.
Hook rate is 3-second video views divided by impressions. Track it per creative to compare openings.
Volume of hooks is cheap. Volume of finished videos is not. Test hooks on the same body first.
d: Say each aloud in under 3 seconds
Add the line as on-screen text
Test 3 hooks on the same body

takeaways: The opening seconds decide whether anything else is seen.
Start with a face, words and the problem.
Track hook rate per creative.
lessons.action: Take your best ad and cut three new versions with different opening lines. Launch them in the same ad set this week.

quiz.q: What does hook rate measure?
options: Share of impressions that became 3-second views
How long the full video is
How many comments the ad got
quiz.explain: Hook rate = 3-second views ÷ impressions. It shows how many people stopped scrolling.

lessons.title: Formats by placement

steps.p: Reels, Stories and Feed show ads at different sizes. A cropped or letterboxed ad looks like an ad and gets skipped.
Make all three for every winner. Most ads only need these.
In Reels and Stories, buttons and captions cover the top and bottom of the screen. Keep the important parts in the middle.
Both have a place. Test both for every new angle.
Shoot vertical with the subject centred, then crop to the other ratios without losing the face or the text.

steps.h: Let each placement get its size
steps.p: Upload the three sizes in the same ad with placement customisation. Meta shows each placement the version that fits.

takeaways: 9:16 for Reels and Stories, 4:5 and 1:1 for Feed.
Keep text and faces out of the top and bottom zones.
Shoot vertical and centred so crops are easy.
lessons.action: Export your current best ad in 9:16, 4:5 and 1:1 and add all three to the same ad using placement customisation.

quiz.q: Which ratio fits Reels and Stories?
quiz.explain: Reels and Stories are full-screen vertical, so 9:16 fills the slot.

lessons.title: Speaking the buyer's language

steps.h: People buy in their own words
steps.p: An ad that sounds like a translation feels foreign. Local words, faces, places and money make people feel the ad was made for them.
A starting point. Cities, ages and regions differ, so test more than one.
Translation swaps words. Localisation changes the whole ad to fit the place.
Write the idea, let a native speaker rewrite it in their own words, then voice it and test it against the original.
Vooads writes and voices ads in Pidgin, Swahili and French and checks them against Meta's rules before you spend. Have a native speaker hear the final cut.
Run this on every ad before it goes to a new geo.
d: A native speaker checks every line

takeaways: Localise the whole ad: words, faces, places and money.
A native speaker should check every line.
Test the local version against the original.
lessons.action: Pick your best English ad and make one localised version for one geo you run. Test both in the same ad set.

quiz.q: What is the difference between translating and localising an ad?
options: Localising adapts words, faces, places and money to the market
quiz.explain: Translation swaps words. Localisation rebuilds the ad so it feels made for that market.

lessons.title: UGC and founder-style videos

steps.p: UGC means user-generated content: ads that look like a normal person filmed them on a phone. They blend into the feed and feel personal.
Studio ads still have uses. UGC tends to fit the feed better and costs less to test.
Rotate through these to find what your audience responds to.
d: Day in the life|routine with app

steps.p: A clear brief saves reshoots. Give the angle, three hook lines, what to say, what never to say, and ask for several takes.
Example: three hooks, two middles and two sizes give twelve ads from one session.
UGC that misleads gets ads rejected and accounts restricted.

takeaways: UGC looks like a post, so people watch it.
A tight brief with hook lines saves reshoots.
Never fake testimonials or promise income.
lessons.action: Write a one-page creator brief for your best angle with three hook lines and a never-say list.

quiz.q: Which of these breaks the rules for honest UGC?
options: A creator saying they earned money guaranteed every day
quiz.explain: Promising guaranteed income is misleading and against ad platform policy. Keep claims honest.

lessons.title: A weekly testing rhythm

steps.p: Teams that test when they feel like it test rarely. Put it on the calendar and it happens every week.
Brief early, launch midweek, read at the end of the week, decide before Monday.
Keep everything the same except the creatives, so the creative is the only reason results differ.
Read from top to bottom. Early numbers tell you about attention. Later ones tell you about money.
d: Cost per FTD once volume allows

steps.p: Illustration: three ads in one test against a $2.00 target cost per join. Ad 1 graduates, Ad 2 holds, Ad 3 retires.
Example: some teams keep a fixed share of spend, such as 20%, for testing so it never stops when budgets get tight.
Every test ends with a decision for each ad.

takeaways: Put testing on the calendar.
Change only the creative so results mean something.
Every ad leaves a test retired or graduated.
lessons.action: Block the testing days in your calendar for the next four weeks and set up one dedicated testing ad set.

quiz.q: Why keep the audience and budget the same across ads in a creative test?
options: So the creative is the only reason results differ
quiz.explain: If audience or budget change too, you cannot tell whether the creative or the setting caused the result.

lessons.title: Spotting creative fatigue

steps.p: The same people see a winning ad again and again. Interest drops and costs climb. That is creative fatigue.
Illustration: frequency rises as the same people see the ad again, and CTR falls. When the lines cross, act.
Frequency is the average number of times each person saw the ad. Watch it with the others.
d: Cost per join up|less for the same spend

steps.p: Example triggers. Set your own numbers and write them into your rules.
d: CTR down a third from its peak
Cost per join over target 3 days
Comments say they have seen it

steps.p: Keep what worked, the angle, and change the parts people are tired of.
A refresh is faster and keeps a proven angle. Replace only when the angle itself is spent.

takeaways: Rising frequency and falling CTR together mean fatigue.
Refresh the hook, face or format and keep the angle.
Write refresh triggers into your rules.
lessons.action: Check frequency and CTR for your top three ads over the last 14 days. Brief a refresh for any ad showing the pattern.

quiz.q: Frequency is rising and CTR is falling on your best ad. What is the first move?
options: Refresh the hook or face and keep the angle
quiz.explain: This is creative fatigue. A refresh keeps the proven angle and gives people something new to look at.

title: Telegram funnels that deposit
description: How Dchessking builds Telegram funnels: channels, bots and join requests, a welcome that gets replies and a 14-day follow-up. Includes how to stay inside Telegram, ad platform and local rules.

lessons.title: Channel, group or bot

steps.p: Channels broadcast, groups let members talk, and bots handle one-to-one conversations. Strong funnels use each for its own job.
Know the strengths before you design the funnel.
A channel is easier to control. A group adds social proof and noise, and needs moderation.
A common setup: the ad sends people to a channel, a bot welcomes them, questions move to DMs, and engaged members are invited to a VIP group.
A bot cannot message someone first. The person must start the bot, or send a join request the bot can answer. Build the funnel around that.
Dchessking on why he runs channels and bots together.
steps.d: The channel holds the audience. The bot holds the conversation. You need both if you want deposits.

steps.p: Start simple. Add a group only when you can moderate it.
d: Group only if you can moderate
One clear next step per stage

takeaways: Channels broadcast, groups talk, bots handle one-to-one.
A bot cannot message someone who has not started it.
Add a group only when you can moderate it.
lessons.action: Draw your current funnel from ad to deposit and mark which step uses a channel, a group and a bot.

quiz.q: Why can a bot not just message every new channel member?
options: Bots are not allowed in channels
A bot can only message people who started it or sent a join request it can answer
quiz.explain: Telegram blocks bots from cold-messaging users. The person must open the conversation first, or send a join request.

lessons.title: The join-request funnel

steps.p: Turn on admin approval for your invite link. Each person sends a request, and your bot gets a chance to speak before they are in.
Unique link per click, request on tap, bot sends a short message, then approves.
The request adds one tap for the user and gives you a lot more control.
Telegram gives the bot a short window to message the person while the request is pending. Use it for a greeting and one easy question.

d.text: Hi Tunde, your request is in. Quick one while I approve it: are you new to trading or already active?
New. I want to learn first
Good place to start. You're in now. Read the pinned post first, it covers the basics in 5 minutes.

steps.p: Illustration: of everyone who requests, some read the message, fewer reply, and those who start the bot can be followed up one-to-one.
Test every step with a second Telegram account before you send ad traffic.
d: Create links with admin approval on
Add your bot as an admin
Log the link and user ID

steps.p: Dchessking on how fast to respond.
steps.d: Every join request is a knock on the door. Answer it like you paid for it, because you did.

takeaways: Join requests give your bot a first message and tracking per link.
Message before approving, then approve fast.
Test the whole flow with a second account.
lessons.action: Create one invite link with admin approval on, connect a bot and run a test request from a second account.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of a join-request link over an open link?
options: It removes the need for a bot
Your bot can greet and check each person before they join
quiz.explain: The request gives the bot a moment to send a message and check the person, and lets you track joins per link.

lessons.title: The welcome message

steps.h: The first message sets the tone
steps.p: The welcome is read by almost everyone who joins. It decides whether they stay, reply and come back tomorrow.
Four parts. Keep it short enough to read on a lock screen.
Example for a trading education channel. Short messages, one idea each, and a question that splits beginners from active traders.

d.text: Welcome, Amina. You joined for the daily market breakdowns. They go out at 8am.
First step: read the pinned guide. It takes about 4 minutes.
One question so I send the right things: have you traded before? Reply yes or no.
No

steps.p: Most weak welcomes try to sell before the person knows where they are.
The answer to the question decides which sequence they get next.
Dchessking on why the welcome deserves real effort.
steps.d: The welcome is the cheapest conversion you will ever get. You already paid for the join.

steps.p: Write yours, then check it against this list.

takeaways: Send the welcome within a minute of the join.
Name, why they came, one step, one question.
Use the answer to choose the next sequence.
lessons.action: Rewrite your welcome to under 60 words with one link and one question. Track the reply rate for a week.

quiz.q: What should the welcome message end with?
quiz.explain: A question gets the first reply, starts the conversation and tells you which follow-up to send.

lessons.title: A 14-day follow-up sequence

steps.p: Most people do not deposit on day one. A planned sequence keeps you in front of them with something useful every day.
Build trust before you sell, then remind without pressure.
Example only. Adjust the days to your product and audience.
One message, one job. Vary the format so people keep opening.
d: One message a day at most
Mix text, voice and short video
Stop selling to people who deposited

steps.p: The difference shows in how many people mute or leave.
Castvoo sends welcome and drip sequences by segment, so each group gets the message written for them. At small scale, a schedule and manual posts work too.
Dchessking on the follow-up.
steps.d: The join is the down payment. The follow-up is where the lead pays you back.

takeaways: Plan 14 days of messages before you buy traffic.
Trust and teaching come before the offer.
Segment, and stop selling to people who already deposited.
lessons.action: Write the titles of 14 messages, one per day, using the example plan. Fill in days 1 to 5 in full this week.

quiz.q: A lead deposited on day 4. What should happen to their sequence?
options: Move them to a depositor sequence and stop the sales messages
quiz.explain: Selling again to someone who already bought wastes their attention. Move them to onboarding and value for depositors.

lessons.title: Turning a VIP group into revenue

steps.p: A VIP group is something people pay for or qualify into. Treat it like a product with a promise, a schedule and quality control.
Be specific about what they get that the free channel does not give.
Invite the people who already engage. A qualifying question finds them.
Example: a $20 monthly VIP that members keep for 4 months on average is worth $80 per member. That tells you what you can spend to bring one in.
People stay when the group is useful every week.
Dchessking on VIP retention.
steps.d: A VIP group keeps paying you only while it keeps earning the members' trust.

steps.p: Simple habits that keep members around.

takeaways: Treat VIP like a product with a clear promise.
Price × months kept = value per member.
Never promise results.
lessons.action: Write the one-sentence promise of your VIP group and list three things members get that the free channel does not.

quiz.q: Members pay $15 a month and stay 6 months on average. What is each member worth?
quiz.explain: $15 × 6 months = $90 per member. That sets how much you can spend to bring one in.

lessons.title: Staying compliant

steps.p: A single banned ad account or reported channel can stop a whole funnel. Following the rules keeps you running.
Check all three before you launch in a new country.
Telegram acts on spam reports. Stay well clear of these.
Risky claims get ads rejected and accounts restricted. Honest claims last.
Five checks, every time, every geo.
These offers are legal in some countries and banned or licensed in others. Ad platforms add their own limits and may need written permission. Check both for every geo.
Dchessking on the cost of shortcuts.
steps.d: I have seen good accounts lost to one lazy claim. No creative is worth the account it runs on.

takeaways: Check Telegram rules, ad policy and local law every time.
Honest claims keep accounts alive.
Trading and gambling need extra checks in every geo.
lessons.action: Review your live ads and channel posts for any profit promise or edited proof and remove it this week.

quiz.q: Which claim is safest to use in a trading ad?
options: Learn how trading works, with the risks explained
quiz.explain: Honest education with risks stated is allowed far more often and does not mislead people.

title: AI Closers and inbox sales
description: Most leads go cold in the inbox. Learn to reply fast, qualify with one question, close with clear scripts and know when a human should take over.

lessons.title: Speed wins the sale

steps.p: Someone who messages you is interested right now. Every minute they wait, they get distracted, check a competitor or forget why they asked.
Illustration: the share of leads who reply back, by how long they waited for your first answer.
An AI Closer answers instantly at any hour and hands harder chats to your team.
Example: the lead writes late at night. The AI answers in seconds, asks one question and gives a next step.

d.text: Hi, how do I start?
Hi Kofi, happy to help. Are you starting small to learn, or have you done this before?
Small, to learn
Then start with this 3-step guide. It takes about 5 minutes. Tell me when you're done and I'll help with the next step.

steps.p: Every chat should move to a next step within the first exchange.
Start by measuring. Most teams are slower than they think.
d: Prepare answers to the top 10 questions
End every reply with a next step

takeaways: Interest fades by the minute.
Cover nights and weekends with an AI first reply.
Every reply ends with a next step.
lessons.action: Message your own funnel from a second account at night and time how long the first reply takes.

quiz.q: Why does reply speed matter so much in inbox sales?
options: Interest is highest when the lead first writes and drops while they wait
Slow replies cost more per message
quiz.explain: The lead is most interested at the moment they write. Waiting gives them time to lose interest or go elsewhere.

lessons.title: Qualifying in one question

steps.p: You do not need a form. One good question tells you who the lead is and which script to use.
Pick one that splits your leads into groups that need different answers.
Example: one question, an honest answer, and the AI changes course to match.

d.text: Quick one so I can help: have you used a trading app before?
Yes but I lost money
Thanks for telling me. Then let's start with the risk guide, it shows how to size trades. Want it?
Yes send it

steps.p: Tag every answer so the next messages, human or AI, fit the person.
Too many questions upfront feels like a form, and people leave.
Write your question, then test it on ten real chats.
d: A different script for each tag

takeaways: One good question tells you which script to use.
Tag every answer.
Help first, then ask more as the chat goes on.
lessons.action: Write one qualifying question for your funnel with two or three button answers, and a short script for each answer.

quiz.q: What makes a good qualifying question?
options: It splits leads into groups that need different answers
It asks for their full name and address
It asks them to pay first
quiz.explain: The point is routing. If every answer leads to the same reply, the question is not doing its job.

lessons.title: Scripts that close

steps.p: A script is a set of answers that move the lead one step at a time. It keeps every reply clear and honest, whoever sends it.
Acknowledge what they said, answer it, reassure honestly, give the next step, then send the link.
Prepare an honest answer for each one before you go live.
Example: answer the doubt directly, point to something they can check themselves, offer a next step.

d.text: Is this a scam?
Fair question. The platform's licence details are on its website, and you control your own account and money. Want the link to check first?
ok send
Here it is. When you're ready, I can walk you through sign-up in 3 steps.

steps.p: Example: clear answer, one link, then a welcome once payment is confirmed.

d.text: How much do I need to start?
The minimum is shown on the platform before you pay. Most people start small while they learn. Here is the sign-up link.
Deposit confirmed
Welcome aboard. Here is your first-day guide.

steps.p: Run every script through this list before it goes live.
d: Pass anything unclear to a human

takeaways: Acknowledge, answer, reassure, next step, link.
Prepare honest answers to the common objections.
Never promise profit.
lessons.action: List the five objections you hear most and write a two-message answer for each.

quiz.q: A lead asks if the offer is a scam. What is the best reply?
options: Ignore it and send the payment link
Answer directly and point to something they can check themselves
quiz.explain: Trust grows when you answer honestly and let them verify. Pushing past the question loses the sale.

lessons.title: Handing off to a human

steps.h: Know when the AI steps back
steps.p: An AI Closer handles most chats. Some need a person: money problems, angry customers, large buyers and anything unclear.

d.b: Hand off at the right moment

steps.p: Write these down so the AI and the team agree on them.
The person who takes over sees the whole chat, so the lead never repeats themselves.
Example: the AI admits the problem, says what happens next and when, and a team member picks it up with full context.

d.text: I paid but nothing showed up
Sorry about that. I'm passing this to a team member now with your details. They will reply within 10 minutes.
Hi, Ada here from the team. I can see your payment from 14:02. Checking it now.

steps.p: A bad handoff makes the lead start again. A good one feels like the same conversation.
Review a few handoffs every week to see if the triggers are right.
d: Promise a time you can keep
Tell the lead who is replying

takeaways: Money issues, anger, large buyers and unclear requests go to a human.
Pass the full history so the lead never repeats themselves.
Promise a reply time you can keep.
lessons.action: Write your four handoff triggers and the exact message the AI sends when it hands over.

quiz.q: Which chat should go to a human?
options: A lead asking for the guide
A lead whose payment went through but nothing appeared
A lead asking the time of the daily post
quiz.explain: Payment problems involve money and trust. A person should take over quickly.

lessons.title: Measuring reply time and close rate

steps.p: Two numbers tell you how your inbox is doing: how fast you reply and how many chats turn into deposits.
Example: 300 chats this week produced 45 deposits, a 15% close rate.
Use the median, the middle value, so one very slow chat does not hide how most chats went.
Illustration: break close rate down by how fast the first reply was. The pattern shows what speed is worth to you.
Four numbers to check every week.
Lost chats teach more than won ones.
d: Find the message where they stopped
Test the change for a week

takeaways: Close rate = deposits ÷ chats.
Track median first reply time.
Read lost chats every week and fix the message where they stop.
lessons.action: Pull last week's chats, work out your close rate and median first reply time, and read 20 chats that did not close.

quiz.q: 200 chats produced 30 deposits. What is the close rate?

title: Scaling Meta in Africa
description: How Dchessking chooses geos, raises budgets, structures campaigns and protects accounts and payments while scaling across African markets. For buyers who already have a profitable campaign.

lessons.title: Picking a geo like an investor

steps.p: Each country has its own costs, payouts, deposit habits and rules. Choose them the way an investor chooses where to put money.
Score each candidate geo on all six before you spend.
Example: return per $1 = payout × FTD rate ÷ cost per join. Above 1, the geo pays back on paper.
Illustration: the same offer scored in three geos. Geo A gets the test budget first.
Hype tells you where other buyers are going. Numbers tell you where you can make money.
If any answer is no, fix it or pick another geo.
d: A native speaker can check ads

steps.p: Dchessking on how he treats a new country.
steps.d: I treat every new geo like a new account at the bank. Small deposit first, then more as it proves itself.

takeaways: Score geos on payout, cost, FTD rate, payments, rules and language.
Payout × FTD rate ÷ cost per join gives a quick return estimate.
Test small before you commit budget.
lessons.action: Score three geos you are considering with the formula, using your best estimates, and pick one to test.

quiz.q: Payout $40, FTD rate 5%, cost per join $1.60. What is the return per $1?
quiz.explain: $40 × 5% = $2.00 value per join. $2.00 ÷ $1.60 = 1.25 back per $1 on paper.

lessons.title: Budget steps

steps.p: Big budget jumps can push an ad set back into learning and make costs swing. Steady steps give you more control.
Many buyers raise a winning budget by about 20% at a time. Treat it as a starting point and learn what your account tolerates.

d.label: raise per step many buyers use

steps.p: Example: starting at $100 a day, three raises of 20% take you to about $173.
Illustration: cost per FTD after steady 20% raises and after a single large jump.
Vertical scaling raises budget on what works. Horizontal scaling copies it into new audiences, creatives or geos.
Example rules. Write your own numbers into the campaign sheet.
d: Raise only after 2 to 3 days on target
Never raise on one good day

steps.p: Dchessking on scaling as a banker.
steps.d: Scaling is lending more to a borrower who has repaid. You lend more only after the last loan came back.

takeaways: Raise budgets in steps. Many buyers use about 20%.
Wait between raises and roll back when costs jump.
Mix vertical and horizontal scaling.
lessons.action: Write your scale rule: when you raise, by how much, how long you wait and when you roll back. Apply it to your best ad set.

quiz.q: An ad set spends $50 a day. Using 20% steps, what is the next budget?

lessons.title: Testing and scaling campaigns

steps.p: Testing looks for winners. Scaling spends on them. Mixing both in one campaign makes each worse.
ABO sets budget per ad set. CBO sets it per campaign and lets Meta split it. Meta now calls CBO Advantage campaign budget.
Winners graduate from testing into a scaling campaign. Testing keeps running alongside.
Keep it simple and let it run.
Using the existing post keeps the likes and comments the ad already earned.
d: Move winners using the post ID

steps.p: Illustration: one way to split spend once you have winners. Adjust to how many new creatives you have.
Dchessking on why he separates the two.
steps.d: Testing is research. Scaling is investing. I used to mix them in one campaign and it burnt money.

takeaways: Run testing and scaling in separate campaigns.
ABO for fair tests, CBO for scaling.
Move winners by post ID to keep social proof.
lessons.action: Split your account into one testing campaign and one scaling campaign and move your current winners using their post IDs.

quiz.q: Why use ABO for creative tests?
options: Each ad set gets its own fixed budget, so tests are fair
quiz.explain: With CBO, Meta may push all spend to one ad early. ABO gives each test a fair share.

lessons.title: Account health and backups

steps.p: Your ad accounts, pages, pixel history and payment methods are the base everything else stands on. Protect them first.

d.b: Protect the base before you scale

steps.p: Each of these can be restricted. Know which you own and who has access.
Most account losses start with weak security or a policy hit.
New accounts often start with a daily spending limit. It tends to rise as you pay on time and stay clear of policy problems.
If one asset fails today, does everything stop?
Buying, renting or borrowing other people's accounts breaks Meta's terms. If an account is restricted, appeal through official channels. Never work around enforcement.

d.b: Own it, appeal it, never dodge it

steps.p: Dchessking on what every buyer needs.
steps.d: Every buyer needs a backup before they need a backup.

takeaways: Two-factor and two admins on everything.
Spending limits tend to grow with clean history.
Own your assets and appeal restrictions through official channels.
lessons.action: List every asset you run on, who has admin access and what the backup is. Fix any asset with one admin or no backup.

quiz.q: An ad account is restricted. What should you do?
options: Open new accounts to keep running the same ads
Appeal through official channels and fix the cause
quiz.explain: Working around enforcement puts the whole business portfolio at risk. Appeal and fix the cause.

lessons.title: Paying for ads from Africa

steps.p: A declined card pauses every ad on the account, often at the worst moment. Payments need the same planning as creatives.
Options differ by country and change over time. Check what Meta offers for your account's currency and country.
Most declines come from limits you can check in advance.
d: FX limits checked with your bank

steps.p: Act the same day. Unpaid balances can hurt account health.
Example: at $300 a day you need about $9,000 a month of card capacity, plus room for currency swings.

steps.h: One card and a payment stack
steps.p: More than one working method keeps ads running when one fails.
Dchessking on the order of work.
steps.d: A winning ad on a declined card makes nothing. Sort payments before you scale.

takeaways: Card limits must sit above your daily spend.
Keep a backup payment method attached.
Plan monthly card capacity before raising budgets.
lessons.action: Check your card's daily and monthly limits against your planned spend for next month and attach a backup method.

quiz.q: You plan to spend $200 a day for 30 days. What monthly card capacity do you need at minimum?
quiz.explain: $200 × 30 = $6,000, plus some room for currency swings.

lessons.title: Going wide to new geos

steps.p: Start new geos with an offer and angle that already work somewhere else. You only change one big thing: the market.

d.b: Copy what works, adapt the rest

steps.p: Take a proven offer and angle, localise them, test with a fixed budget, then scale what holds.
Examples of markets that share a language. Always check law and ad policy first.
Set all of this before day one.
d: Fixed test budget and kill rules

steps.p: The same ad dropped into a new country often underperforms the original.
Example: cap yourself at a few new geos at once so you can read each one properly.
Dchessking on expanding.
steps.d: Every new geo starts as a test deposit. Only the ones that prove themselves get real money.

takeaways: Expand with offers and angles that already work.
Localise, then test with fixed budgets and kill rules.
Test a few geos at a time so you can read them.
lessons.action: Pick one neighbouring geo for your best campaign, confirm the law and ad policy, and brief one localised creative.

quiz.q: What should stay the same when you test a new geo?
quiz.explain: Keep the proven offer and angle and change the market. Then localise language, prices and faces.

title: Affiliate offers and payouts
description: Payout models, offer terms, break-even maths and how to negotiate with networks using your own data. Read an offer properly before you spend a dollar on it.

lessons.title: CPA, RevShare or hybrid

steps.h: How you are paid shapes everything
steps.p: The payout model decides your cash flow, your risk and how long you wait to see your money back.

d.b: Pick the model before the offer

steps.p: CPA pays once per qualifying FTD. RevShare pays a share of the revenue the brand earns from your players over time. Hybrid mixes both.
CPA suits buyers who need cash back fast. RevShare suits buyers who can wait and send players who stay.
Illustration: total earned from one player under CPA and under RevShare. RevShare starts lower and can pass CPA later, or never.
Example: a $30 CPA plus 25% RevShare gives some cash now and some upside later.
Negative carryover means losses in one month are deducted from next month's RevShare. Ask about it before you sign.

takeaways: CPA pays once and fast. RevShare pays over time.
Hybrid gives some of each.
Ask about negative carryover before choosing RevShare.
lessons.action: For your main offer, write down which model you are on and whether a different model would suit your cash flow better.

quiz.q: You need your spend back within weeks to keep buying. Which model fits best?
quiz.explain: CPA pays a fixed amount soon after the FTD qualifies, so cash returns faster.

lessons.title: Reading offer terms

steps.p: Two offers with the same payout can be very different once you read the KPIs, holds, caps and banned traffic.
Every one of these can change what you actually get paid.
Get the answers in writing before you send traffic.
d: What counts as a qualifying FTD?

steps.p: Vague terms usually get clearer only after a payout is cut.
KPIs are checked after traffic is sent. Missing them can mean payouts are cut or held.
Trading and gambling offers must be legal in the country you target and allowed by the ad platform there. A high payout in a geo you cannot run is a liability.

d.b: Check law and ad policy per geo

takeaways: KPIs, holds, caps and banned traffic change the real payout.
Get every term in writing.
Only run trading and gambling where they are legal and allowed.
lessons.action: Take your current offer and write the answers to the five questions. Ask your manager for anything you cannot answer.

quiz.q: Why does the hold period matter?
options: It decides how long your money is tied up before you are paid
quiz.explain: During the hold you have already paid for traffic but not been paid. Longer holds need more cash to keep running.

lessons.title: The break-even maths

steps.h: Know the line before you cross it
steps.p: Break-even is the most you can pay and still not lose money. Above it, every sale costs you.
Your break-even CPA is the payout minus your other costs per FTD, such as tools, creatives and fees.
Example: an $80 payout with a 3% FTD rate means each join is worth $2.40.
Example: at $140 a day with a 30-day hold, about $4,200 of spend is waiting to be paid back at any time.
Illustration: margin per FTD on an $80 payout as your cost per FTD rises.
Break-even maths only helps if the inputs are real.

takeaways: Max CPA = payout minus other costs per FTD.
Value per join = payout × FTD rate.
Holds tie up cash. Plan for them.
lessons.action: Build a one-line break-even model for your offer with payout, FTD rate, other costs and hold period.

quiz.q: Payout is $70 and other costs are $10 per FTD. What is your break-even CPA?
quiz.explain: $70 − $10 = $60. Above $60 per FTD you lose money.

lessons.title: Negotiating with data

steps.p: Networks pay more to affiliates who send steady, good-quality players. Your numbers are what prove you are one.
A short report beats a long message.
A specific request with data behind it is easier for a manager to approve.
Prove quality, show volume, ask for one number, agree a test period and review.
Example: a $5 raise on 100 FTDs a week is $500 a week more. Know your number before the call.
Ask from strength and keep your word afterwards.
d: One specific number to ask for

takeaways: Negotiate with several weeks of data.
Ask for one specific number.
Get it in writing and deliver what you promised.
lessons.action: Prepare a one-page summary of your last 4 to 8 weeks on your main offer: FTDs, quality against KPIs and planned volume.

quiz.q: What makes a payout request most likely to succeed?
options: Weeks of data showing quality and a specific ask
Sending more traffic without telling them
quiz.explain: Managers approve raises they can justify. Data and a clear number give them that.

lessons.title: Managing network relationships

steps.p: A good affiliate manager can bring you early offers, better terms and help when something breaks. Treat the relationship as part of the business.
Small, regular contact builds trust.
These cost little and pay off when you need help.
d: Work with more than one network

steps.p: Networks remember who was easy to work with.
Illustration: revenue split across sources. One network changing terms should not stop the business.
Build a second and third source while the first is still working.

takeaways: Send short, regular updates with numbers.
Keep every agreement in writing.
Work with more than one network.
lessons.action: Send your affiliate manager a short weekly update this Friday with FTDs, quality notes and next week's plan.

quiz.q: Why work with more than one network?
options: So one network's changes do not stop your business
Networks pay more if you have many
quiz.explain: Offers get paused and terms change. More than one source keeps you running.

title: The operator playbook: running a buying team
description: How Dchessking hires, trains and manages media buyers at Zedapex. SOPs, naming, daily reports, budget allocation and the risk controls that keep accounts safe.

lessons.title: Hiring and testing media buyers

steps.p: Tools can be taught in a week. Judgment, honesty and discipline with money take much longer. Hire for those.
A strong buyer shows all four in a paid test.
Each step filters before you put real money in someone's hands.
Keep it small, fixed and written down so you judge process as well as results.
Watch how they report as much as what they report.
Example: a fixed test budget per candidate. Set an amount you can afford to lose completely.
Dchessking on what he looks for.
steps.d: I hire buyers who report their losses honestly. Anyone can show you a winner.

takeaways: Hire for judgment, honesty and discipline.
Use a small, fixed, written paid test.
Judge how candidates report as well as what they make.
lessons.action: Write a one-page paid test brief: budget, offer, geo, rules, duration and what you will judge.

quiz.q: What matters most in a candidate's paid test?
options: Process, honesty in reporting and the numbers
How fast they spent the budget
quiz.explain: One test can be lucky or unlucky. Process and honest reporting predict how they will handle real budgets.

lessons.title: SOPs and naming conventions

steps.p: An SOP, or standard operating procedure, is a written checklist for a repeated task. It lets any buyer do the job the same way.

d.b: Written once, done the same way

steps.p: Use the same order everywhere so names can be sorted and filtered.
Example: Kenya, Swahili, hook 7, launched 6 October 2026, by buyer EJ.
Start with the tasks that cost the most when done wrong.
d: What to do after a ban

steps.p: SOPs make results depend less on who is working that day.
SOPs change as the platforms change. Review them on a schedule.
Dchessking on where his SOPs came from.
steps.d: My best systems came from mistakes I did not want to pay for twice.

takeaways: SOPs make repeated work consistent.
One naming convention, used everywhere.
Review SOPs monthly.
lessons.action: Write your naming convention and rename every live campaign in one account to match it.

quiz.q: Why use a fixed naming convention?
options: Names can be sorted and filtered, and anyone can read them
quiz.explain: A shared format means anyone on the team can find, filter and understand any campaign at a glance.

lessons.title: The daily report

steps.p: The daily report is how the team sees the business. One template, one deadline, every day.
Short, numeric and comparable from day to day.
Reports are only useful if someone reads them and acts the same day.
Illustration: ROAS by buyer for one week. The report shows where to look first.
Rules that keep reports honest and useful.
A useful report answers: what happened, why, and what you did.
Dchessking on why the report is daily.
steps.d: The daily report is the bank statement. Skip it and you find out about losses late.

takeaways: One template, one deadline, every day.
Spend, joins, FTDs, revenue, actions and issues.
Someone reads it and decides the same day.
lessons.action: Create a daily report template with the six sections and ask every buyer to submit it by a fixed time for one week.

quiz.q: What makes a daily report useful?
options: The same format daily, with totals, targets, actions and reasons
quiz.explain: Consistency lets you compare days, and actions with reasons let you check decisions.

lessons.title: Allocating budget across buyers

steps.p: Budget is the team's capital. Give more to buyers who return it reliably and less to those still proving themselves.
Equal splits feel fair but fund losses. Performance splits reward results and need guardrails.
Example: look at ROAS and how steady it was across the whole week.
Illustration: one week's split across three buyers after the review.
Same day each week, same steps.
Guardrails stop one lucky week from moving too much money.
d: Reward process as well as results
Give new buyers a fixed ramp

steps.p: Dchessking on funding buyers.
steps.d: I fund buyers the way a bank funds borrowers. Track record first, then size.

takeaways: Budget is capital. Fund steady returns.
Use floors, caps and steps as guardrails.
Review allocation on the same day every week.
lessons.action: Rank your buyers by last week's ROAS and consistency, then set next week's budget with a cap per buyer.

quiz.q: Buyer C had one great day and four losing days. What should happen to their budget?
options: Double it because of the great day
Judge the whole week and move budget in small steps
quiz.explain: One day is noise. Use the week's results and change budgets gradually.

lessons.title: Risk, compliance and protecting accounts

steps.p: One banned business portfolio or leaked login can stop the whole team. Risk controls are part of the job.
Write a response for each before it happens.
Give each person only what they need, and take it back the day they leave.
d: Remove access the day someone leaves

steps.p: Every creative passes the same checks before launch. Trading and gambling need the law and the ad platform's rules checked for each geo.
Prepared teams lose a day when something breaks. Reactive teams lose weeks.
Stop spend, appeal through official channels, write down what happened and update the SOP. Never work around enforcement with new accounts.
Dchessking on what matters most.
steps.d: Traffic banking only works while the bank stays open. Protect the accounts first.

takeaways: Personal logins, least access, 2FA and monthly audits.
Every creative passes a claims and policy check.
Handle bans with appeals and SOP updates, never workarounds.
lessons.action: Audit who has admin access to every ad account and page you run. Remove anyone who no longer needs it.

quiz.q: A buyer leaves the team today. When should their access be removed?
quiz.explain: Remove access the same day. Old access is one of the most common ways accounts get compromised.
